39	
40	```
41	cat ~/.jenkins/secrets/initialAdminPassword
42	```
43	
44	**Linux:** follow the [official Jenkins Linux install
45	instructions](https://www.jenkins.io/doc/book/installing/linux/) for your
46	distro (e.g. the `apt`/`yum` package repo), then start it via `systemctl
47	start jenkins` (most distros enable/start it automatically on install).
48	`JENKINS_HOME` is `/var/lib/jenkins` by default. Get the initial admin
49	password with:
50	
51	```
52	sudo cat /var/lib/jenkins/secrets/initialAdminPassword
53	```
54	
55	**Both:** Jenkins listens on `http://localhost:8080`. Open it, paste the
56	password, and install the "suggested plugins" set when prompted.
57	
58	## 2. Install additional plugins
59	
60	Manage Jenkins → Plugins → Available plugins, install:
61	
62	- **GitHub Branch Source** — lets Jenkins discover branches/PRs on a GitHub
63	  repo and is the GitHub equivalent of the Bitbucket Branch Source plugin
64	  SUNDIALS uses.
65	- **Collapsing Console Sections** (optional) — collapses long build log
66	  sections for readability, same as SUNDIALS' setup.
67	
68	## 3. Add a GitHub credential
69	
70	Jenkins needs read access to `gkeyllorg/gkeyll` to poll for branches and PRs:
71	
72	1. Create a GitHub Personal Access Token with `repo` scope (Settings →
73	   Developer settings → Personal access tokens on GitHub).
74	2. In Jenkins: Manage Jenkins → Credentials → System → Global credentials →
75	   Add Credentials → kind "GitHub personal access token" (or "Username with
76	   password", username = your GitHub username, password = the token).
77	
78	## 3a. Scope your controller to its own nodes
79	
80	`ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile` has a single `nodes` map listing every known build
81	node across every independent controller that builds this repo (yours and
82	anyone else's). This keeps that map a shared, PR-reviewable source of truth
83	— but it also means your controller must be told which of those labels it
84	actually owns agents for, or it will try to start a `node(label)` block for
85	someone else's node and hang forever waiting for an executor that will never
86	exist under your controller.
87	
88	Manage Jenkins → System → Global properties → check "Environment variables"
89	→ Add:
90	
91	- Name: `CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS`
92	- Value: a comma-separated list of the node label(s) *this controller* owns,
93	  e.g. `manauref_lt1`, or `alice_laptop,alice_workstation` if you register
94	  more than one node under your own controller.
95	
96	This is a controller-wide setting — set it once, regardless of how many
97	nodes your controller owns. If it's unset (or blank), the pipeline fails
98	fast with an error telling you to set it, rather than hanging; that's
99	expected the first time you set up a new controller.
100	
101	## 4. Add a build node
102	
103	Every machine that runs builds — including the controller's own machine — is
104	a Jenkins "node" with a label matching one used in `ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`'s
105	`nodes` map. This procedure is the same whether you're setting up
106	`manauref_lt1` (the first node) or adding another machine later.
107	
108	### 4.1. Register the node and label it
109	
110	- **This machine** (the controller itself, e.g. `manauref_lt1`): Manage
111	  Jenkins → Nodes → "Built-In Node" → Configure → Labels: add the label.
112	- **A separate machine** (e.g. a workstation): Manage Jenkins → Nodes → New
113	  Node → "Permanent Agent" → Launch method "Launch agents via SSH",
114	  host/credentials for that machine, and give it a label. Nothing to install
115	  there yourself — Jenkins pushes its agent jar over SSH. Make sure Java, a
116	  C/C++/Fortran toolchain, and `cmake` are present; `mkdeps` builds everything
117	  else from scratch per build.
118	
119	This label is what the Jenkinsfile's `node('<label>')` matches.
120	
121	### 4.2. Fix the node's `PATH`
122	
123	On **macOS**, Jenkins runs as a `launchd` service (via `brew services`),
124	which does **not** source your shell profile (`~/.zshrc`, `~/.zprofile`) —
125	so it starts with launchd's bare-bones default `PATH`
126	(`/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`) and can't find Homebrew tools like `cmake`,
127	even though `which cmake` works fine in your terminal.
128	
129	On **Linux**, the built-in node's agent process is started by `systemd`
130	(via the `jenkins` service), which likewise does not source your shell
131	profile — it uses whatever minimal `PATH` is baked into the unit's
132	environment, which typically misses anything installed under `/opt`, a
133	package manager outside the base distro repos, or `$HOME`. An SSH-launched
134	agent on another machine (either OS) has its own, similar set of environment
135	quirks to sort out, since `sshd` non-interactive sessions don't source
136	`~/.bashrc`/`~/.zshrc` either.
137	
138	Fix this per-node in Jenkins itself (not by editing the launchd plist,
139	systemd unit, or a shell profile) so it works the same way regardless of how
140	each node's agent process is started, and each node keeps its own value —
141	this generalizes cleanly as you add more, across OSes.
142	
143	Manage Jenkins → Nodes → `<label>` → Configure → Node Properties → check
144	"Environment variables" → Add:
145	
146	- Name: `PATH`
147	- Value: wherever this node's build tools (`cmake`, compilers, MPI, a
148	  `python` with `numpy`, etc.) actually live, e.g.:
149	  - macOS (`manauref_lt1`):
150	    `/opt/homebrew/bin:/opt/homebrew/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`
151	  - Linux: typically
152	    `/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`, plus anywhere your
153	    toolchain/MPI/Python were installed outside the base distro repos (e.g.
154	    `/opt/<something>/bin`, a Conda/venv `bin`, or `/usr/local/cuda/bin`).
155	
156	Don't assume this matches another node's value — especially across OSes.
157	
158	### 4.3. Personal machine or team machine?
159	
160	- **Personal computer** (like `manauref_lt1`): the multibranch job builds —
161	  i.e. executes — the code of any PR opened against the repo, on whichever
162	  node picks it up. On a personal machine you probably don't want to run
163	  other contributors' PR code, so restrict this node to PRs you authored: in
164	  `ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`, add `allowedPrAuthors: ['<your-github-username>']`
165	  to this node's entry in the `nodes` map. PR builds from any other author
166	  are skipped on this node (logged in the console, not failed); builds of
167	  `main` itself are unaffected, since there's no PR author to check there.
168	  Note this is a Jenkinsfile-level control, not a GitHub-side protection — it
169	  only takes effect once Jenkins has already scanned and started that node's
170	  branch of the pipeline.
171	- **Shared/team machine**: omit `allowedPrAuthors` from its entry — it will
172	  build PRs from anyone.
173	
174	### 4.4. Register the node in the Jenkinsfile
175	
176	Add (or confirm) an entry in the `nodes` map in `ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`,
177	using whichever `mkdeps`/`configure` scripts under `machines/` match that
178	node's OS:
179	
180	```groovy
181	def nodes = [
182	    'manauref_lt1': [mkdeps: 'mkdeps.macos.sh', configure: 'configure.macos.sh', allowedPrAuthors: ['manauref']],
183	    'workstation-node': [mkdeps: 'mkdeps.linux.sh', configure: 'configure.linux.cpu.sh'],
184	]
185	```
186	
187	Commit and push (a normal PR against `main`, same as any other change).
188	Adding a node's entry to this shared map doesn't by itself make any
189	controller build on it — only a controller whose `CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS`
190	(step 3a) includes this label will. The next PR build will then run on every
191	node your controller owns, in parallel (subject to each node's
192	`allowedPrAuthors`, if set).
193	
194	## 5. Nothing to pre-build
195	
196	Unlike an earlier version of this setup, the pipeline does **not** assume a
197	pre-built `gkylsoft/` on any node. Each build passes
198	`PREFIX=$WORKSPACE/gkylsoft` to that node's `mkdeps`/`configure` scripts, so
199	dependencies are built from scratch inside that build's own Jenkins
200	workspace — isolated from any manual checkout you have elsewhere, and safe
201	for concurrent builds of different branches/PRs on the same node (each gets
202	its own workspace, so its own `gkylsoft/`).
203	
204	The tradeoff is build time: expect each build to spend several extra minutes
205	building SuperLU/LuaJIT from source before it even gets to compiling Gkeyll,
206	same as `.github/workflows/mac_build.yml` does on GitHub's runners.
207	
208	You still need a working toolchain, `cmake`, and a `python` on `PATH` with
209	`numpy` installed (used to process the ADAS atomic data some gyrokinetic
210	unit tests, e.g. `ctest_dg_iz`/`ctest_dg_recomb`, need at runtime) on each
211	node for its `mkdeps` script to succeed — if you've built Gkeyll manually on
212	that machine before, you already have most of these:
213	
214	- **macOS**: Xcode command line tools (`xcode-select --install`) for the
215	  C/C++/Fortran toolchain, plus `cmake`/`python` (e.g. via Homebrew).
216	- **Linux**: a C/C++/Fortran toolchain (e.g. `build-essential` + `gfortran`
217	  on Debian/Ubuntu, or the equivalent group on your distro), plus `cmake` and
218	  a `python` with `numpy` from your package manager (or a Conda/venv install,
219	  as long as it's on the `PATH` set in step 4.2).
220	
221	## 6. Create the multibranch pipeline job
222	
223	New Item → name it (e.g. `gkeyll`) → **Multibranch Pipeline**.
224	
225	- **Branch Sources** → Add source → GitHub:
226	  - Credentials: the one added in step 3.
227	  - Repository HTTPS URL: `https://github.com/gkeyllorg/gkeyll`
228	  - Behaviors: "Discover branches" (at least `main`) and "Discover pull
229	    requests from origin". Add "Discover pull requests from forks" only if
230	    external contributors submit PRs from forks.
231	- **Build Configuration** → Mode: "by Jenkinsfile", Script Path:
232	  `ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`.
233	- **Scan Multibranch Pipeline Triggers** → check "Periodically if not
234	  otherwise run" → interval **2 minutes**.
235	
236	If your controller is behind NAT (as `manauref_lt1`'s is), GitHub can't push
237	a webhook to it. The periodic scan above is how Jenkins learns about
238	new/updated PRs instead — every 2 minutes it asks GitHub for changes and
239	kicks off a build if there are any. This means there's up to a ~2 minute
240	delay before a build starts, which is an acceptable tradeoff for not having
241	to run a public tunnel (e.g. ngrok) just to receive webhooks. If your
242	controller has a reachable public address, you can set up a GitHub webhook
243	instead for near-instant triggering — not covered here since none of our
244	controllers currently need it.
245	
246	Save. Jenkins will scan the repo, find `main` and any open PRs with a
247	Jenkinsfile, and start building them.
248	
249	## What the pipeline does
250	
251	First, the pipeline filters the shared `nodes` map down to just the label(s)
252	in this controller's own `CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS` (step 3a) — failing fast if
253	that's not set. Then, per node this controller owns, in parallel (skipping a
254	node entirely if the PR's author isn't in that node's `allowedPrAuthors`,
255	when set):
256	
257	1. `printenv` — for debugging the build environment.
258	2. `make clean` and `rm -rf $WORKSPACE/gkylsoft` — the workspace persists
259	   across builds for a given branch/PR, so without this, a stale or (e.g.
260	   from a prior interrupted or racing build) corrupted file can look
261	   up-to-date and never get rebuilt/reinstalled, silently breaking the link
262	   or mixing old and new dependency files. Wiping both every run makes each
263	   build genuinely from scratch.
264	3. That node's `mkdeps` script (e.g. `machines/mkdeps.macos.sh`) — builds
265	   `gkylsoft/` from scratch into `$WORKSPACE/gkylsoft`.
266	4. That node's `configure` script (e.g. `machines/configure.macos.sh`) —
267	   generates `config.mak` pointing at that freshly-built `gkylsoft/`.
268	5. `make -j3 check` — builds **and runs** all unit tests (`core`, `moments`,
269	   `vlasov`, `gyrokinetic`, `pkpm`); a failing unit test fails the build.
270	6. `make -j3 regression` — builds (does not execute) all regression tests,
271	   matching today's `.github/workflows/mac_build.yml` scope. There is no
272	   automated regression-test runner yet; running a curated subset of
273	   regression tests is a follow-up.
274	7. Archives `build/**/*.log` so logs are downloadable from the Jenkins build
275	   page even on failure.
276

1	# Support independent Jenkins controllers, without cross-controller SSH
2	
3	## Context
4	
5	`ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile` currently assumes exactly one Jenkins controller. Its
6	`nodes` map is a single, shared list of every known build node (label ->
7	mkdeps/configure/allowedPrAuthors), and the pipeline's `parallel(branches)`
8	tries to run a `node(label) { ... }` block for *every* entry in that map,
9	unconditionally.
10	
11	This breaks as soon as a second person wants to run their own Jenkins
12	controller against the same repo/Jenkinsfile: their controller only has
13	agents for their own node label(s), but the shared `nodes` map still lists
14	`manauref_lt1` (and any others), so their controller would try to run a
15	`node('manauref_lt1')` block too — and hang forever waiting for an executor
16	that will never show up under their controller.
17	
18	The alternative — add the new person's machine as a node *under* the existing
19	controller (via SSH launch) — was rejected: that requires the existing
20	controller to have SSH access into their machine, which they may not want to
21	grant. So each person needs to be able to run their own, fully independent
22	Jenkins controller: own install, own GitHub credential, own multibranch job
23	— with no SSH trust relationship between controllers required.
24	
25	The goal of this plan is to let the `nodes` map stay a single, shared,
26	PR-reviewable source of truth (so everyone can see who's running CI on what,
27	with which mkdeps/configure/allowedPrAuthors) while letting each independent
28	controller safely run *only* the subset of nodes it actually owns, without
29	hanging on labels it doesn't have.
30	
31	## Approach: controller scopes itself via one global env var
32	
33	Keep one canonical `Jenkinsfile` and one canonical `nodes` map (no per-person
34	Jenkinsfile forks, no Shared Library needed — `buildAndTest` stays exactly as
35	it is). Add a filtering step: before building the `parallel` map, the
36	Jenkinsfile reads a comma-separated list of node labels *this controller
37	owns* from a controller-level global environment variable, and restricts
38	itself to just those entries. Every controller runs the exact same
39	Jenkinsfile from the exact same multibranch job pointed at
40	`ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`, but each is configured (once, locally, outside the
41	repo) with which labels are actually its own.
42	
43	This is analogous to how each *node's* `PATH` is already set via a local
44	Jenkins Node Property rather than committed to the repo (see README step
45	4.2) — here it's a controller-wide property instead of a per-node one.
46	
47	Concretely: a new env var `CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS` (Manage Jenkins → System →
48	Global properties → Environment variables), e.g. `CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS=manauref_lt1`
49	on your controller. A second person's controller would set
50	`CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS=alice_laptop` and add their own `alice_laptop` entry to
51	the same shared `nodes` map via a normal PR.
52	
53	If the var is unset or empty, fail the build immediately with a clear error
54	rather than silently defaulting to "try every node" (which is exactly the
55	hang this plan exists to prevent) or "build nothing" (which would look like
56	a silent CI outage). This makes the missing-configuration case loud and
57	self-explanatory instead of a mysterious hang.
58	
59	## Changes
60	
61	**`ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`**
62	- After the `nodes` map definition, add:
63	  ```groovy
64	  // Every controller running this Jenkinsfile shares the same `nodes` map
65	  // above, but only owns a subset of those labels as actual agents. Each
66	  // controller declares its own subset via a global environment variable
67	  // (Manage Jenkins -> System -> Global properties -> Environment variables),
68	  // set once locally and NOT committed to the repo -- see ci/jenkins/README.md.
69	  // Without this, a controller would try node(label) for a label it has no
70	  // agent for and hang forever waiting for an executor that will never exist.
71	  def ownedLabels = (env.CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS ?: '').split(',').collect { it.trim() }.findAll { it }
72	  if (!ownedLabels) {
73	      error("CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS is not set on this controller (Manage Jenkins -> System -> Global properties -> Environment variables). Set it to a comma-separated list of the node label(s) this controller owns, e.g. 'manauref_lt1'. See ci/jenkins/README.md.")
74	  }
75	  def myNodes = nodes.findAll { label, cfg -> ownedLabels.contains(label) }
76	  ```
77	- Change `nodes.collectEntries { ... }` to `myNodes.collectEntries { ... }` so
78	  the `parallel` map is built only from this controller's own nodes. No other
79	  change to the closure body, `buildAndTest`, or anything downstream.
80	- Update the comment above the `nodes` map to note that it's shared across
81	  every independent controller building this repo, and that a given
82	  controller only acts on the subset named in its own `CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS`.
83	
84	**`ci/jenkins/README.md`**
85	- Intro paragraph: add a short note that this doc covers both (a) adding a
86	  node under an *existing* controller, and (b) setting up your *own*,
87	  independent controller — and that either is fine; pick (b) if you don't
88	  want to grant the existing controller's admin SSH access to your machine.
89	- New step, added right after step 3 (GitHub credential) and before step 4
90	  (Add a build node) — call it **"3a. Scope your controller to its own
91	  nodes"** (or fold into a renumbered step; exact numbering decided when
92	  writing) — explaining:
93	  - Every controller runs from the same `ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile` and the same
94	    shared `nodes` map in it, but must only claim the node label(s) it
95	    actually has agents for.
96	  - Set `CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS` under Manage Jenkins → System → Global
97	    properties → Environment variables to a comma-separated list of your
98	    label(s), e.g. `manauref_lt1`, or `alice_laptop,alice_workstation` if you
99	    register more than one node under your own controller.
100	  - If this is unset, the pipeline fails fast with an error telling you to
101	    set it — this is expected the first time you set up a new controller.
102	  - This is a controller-wide setting, so it only needs to be set once per
103	    controller regardless of how many nodes that controller owns.
104	- Step 4 ("Add a build node") stays as-is (already generic/personal-vs-team
105	  aware); add one line to step 4.4 clarifying that adding your node's entry
106	  to the shared `nodes` map (via a normal PR against `main`) is independent
107	  of which controller runs it — that's what `CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS` (previous
108	  step) controls, locally, per controller.
109	- "What the pipeline does" section: add a leading bullet noting the
110	  `CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS` filtering happens before the per-node parallel
111	  stages described below.
112	
113	## Verification
114	
115	- Inspect the diff by eye (no local Groovy linter available); `split`,
116	  `collect`, `findAll`, `contains` are common Groovy GDK methods already used
117	  elsewhere in this file (`collectEntries`, `contains` are already present),
118	  so no new script-security sandbox approval is expected — but note in the
119	  README's troubleshooting that if Jenkins ever reports a
120	  "script not yet approved" error for one of these, it's fixed via Manage
121	  Jenkins → In-process Script Approval (a one-time, per-controller step),
122	  matching a pattern we've already hit once before in this setup.
123	- On your existing `manauref_lt1` controller: set
124	  `CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS=manauref_lt1`, push the Jenkinsfile change, and
125	  confirm the next PR build still runs on `manauref_lt1` exactly as before
126	  (regression check that filtering to a single-entry allowlist is a no-op
127	  for the existing single-controller setup).
128	- Confirm the fail-fast path: temporarily unset/blank `CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS`
129	  on a scratch job or note it as a known manual check, and confirm the build

Repo layout note: the git root is `/Users/mfrancis/Documents/gkeyll/code/gkeyll_v0/gkeyll`. ## 1. `gkeyll/lua/Tool/runregression.lua` — full behavior

This is a self-contained Lua CLI tool (parsed with `Lib.argparse`) that is invoked as `gkeyll runregression <command> ...` (it runs inside the `gkeyll` Lua interpreter/executable, requiring `lfs`, `sqlite3`, etc. — i.e. it needs the *installed* `gkeyll` binary, not just build artifacts). Header comment (lines 1–19) summarizes the design:

- **Discovery**: Lua tests are discovered from `<source_dir>/<layer>/luareg/rt_*.lua`; C tests from `<source_dir>/<layer>/creg/rt_*.c`. Layers are `moments`, `vlasov`, `gyrokinetic`, `pkpm` (line 48–53); `core` is NOT a layer runregression scans (no `core/luareg`, and `core/creg` isn't scanned either, even though `core/creg` has 9 `rt_*.c` files built by `make regression`).
- **Lua tests** run via `gkeyll <file>` from a per-test scratch dir (`prepareLuaRun`, lines 932–964).
- **C tests** are compiled on the fly per test: `cp` the `.c` source plus the **installed** `share/Makefile` (`<prefix>/gkeyll/share/Makefile`, produced by `make install` — see §3) into a scratch dir and run `make <testname>` there (`compileCTest`, lines 894–926). This explicitly requires `make install` to have been run (error message at lines 898–903: *"Ensure 'make install' has been run for the current build."*). **No separate `make regression` step is needed** for runregression's own C-test path (explicitly stated in the header and again in the CLI `--description`, lines 2171–2173).

**Hard dependency**: requires SQLite3 (lines 24–28) — if `GKYL_HAVE_SQLITE3 == false` it prints an error and returns 1. In practice SQLite3 is bundled (`core/minus/sqlite3.c`, compiled into `libg0core` per `core/Makefile-core`), and nothing in the repo ever sets `GKYL_HAVE_SQLITE3 = false`, so this should not be an obstacle.

**Commands** (argparse tree, lines 2152–2273):
- `configure -s/--source-dir <path> [-p/--prefix] [-m/--mpiexec] [--drop-tables]` — required first step; creates `<prefix>/gkeyll-results/<layer>/{regressiondb, luareg-runs, luareg-accepted, creg-runs, creg-accepted}` and writes `<prefix>/gkeyll-results/runregression.config.lua` (falls back to `~/runregression.config.lua` for legacy configs). `--source-dir` must be the gkeyll repo root (parent of `moments/`, `vlasov/`, etc.).
- `list [-r/--run-only NAME] [-a/--all] [-m/--moat] [-c/--c-only] [-l/--lua-only]` — prints discovered tests without running them.
- `run [layer] [check|create] [options]` — the main entry point. A layer name (`moments`/`vlasov`/`gyrokinetic`/`pkpm`) can be injected before `check`/`create`, e.g. `gkeyll runregression run moments check` (pre-parsed manually at lines 123–142 since argparse doesn't support this natively).
  - `check` — compare outputs to accepted baselines, record pass/fail in DB.
  - `create` — run tests and save output as the new accepted baseline (always forces CPU mode on GPU builds for determinism).
  - No subcommand — tests run, but results are neither saved nor compared (status = -1 "skip").
  - Options: `-r/--run-only NAME[,NAME...]` (bare name, absolute path, or directory), `-a/--all` (bypass ignore lists), `-m/--moat` (run only the curated **MOAT = "Mother Of All Tests"** subset — see §2/§5), `-c/--c-only`, `-l/--lua-only`, `-t/--timeout SECS` (default 0 = unlimited; per-test kill via `timeout`/`gtimeout`/Perl-fork fallback, lines 85–102, 310–366), `--gpu-tol` (default `1e-7`, for GPU-vs-accepted / CPU-vs-GPU comparisons), `--no-gpu` (skip GPU even on GPU build), `-j/--jobs N` (default 1 = serial; `0` = auto-detect physical CPU count via `sysctl`/`nproc`, lines 104–121; concurrent execution via shell background jobs, `executeBatch`, lines 1044–1102; C compilation and GPU variants always run serially).
- `listunit` / `rununit` — separate unit-test runner (Lua `test_*.lua` and compiled `ctest_*` executables under `<layer>/unit/`), distinct from regression.

**No explicit `-h`/help text is hand-written inline** beyond argparse's auto-generated `--help` (argparse library generates usage from the `:description`/`:option`/`:flag` calls above); the tool's own top-level `:description(...)` (lines 2157–2174) doubles as usage documentation and gives the canonical workflow:
```
1. make install -j4
2. gkeyll runregression configure --source-dir /absolute/path/to/gkeyll/
3. gkeyll runregression run create --timeout 120
4. gkeyll runregression run check  --timeout 120
5. gkeyll runregression run moments check
```

**Comparison/tolerance logic** (`compareFiles`, lines 1190–1298): uses the `G0.Zero` Lua-C API (registered by `gkyl_zero_lw_openlibs`, `core/apps/zero_lw.c`) to diff `.gkyl` output files — `dynvector` diff, `block-topology` diff, or grid+array diff via `gkyl_array_diff`/`rectGridCmp`. Default tolerance is `absTol=relTol=1e-12` for CPU-vs-accepted; a looser `--gpu-tol` (default `1e-7`) is used for GPU-related comparisons. A failure requires **both** abs and rel tolerance to be exceeded (avoids false positives near zero / at large magnitude). Failures are logged with per-file diff magnitudes and written to `<runDir>/_rr_failures.txt`.

**Side effects**:
- Writes `.gkyl` output files into per-test scratch directories under `<prefix>/gkeyll-results/<layer>/{luareg,creg}-runs/<test>/`.
- `create` copies outputs into `.../{luareg,creg}-accepted/<test>/` as the new baseline (this is a mutation of tracked "golden" data on the machine's `gkylsoft` prefix, not in the git repo).
- Writes/updates a SQLite DB per layer at `<results_dir>/<layer>/regressiondb` (schema at lines 221–249: `RegressionMeta` per-run summary, `RegressionData` per-test result incl. status codes: `-4` compile_fail, `-3` timeout, `-2` create, `-1` skip, `0` fail, `1` pass; plus GPU columns).
- With `--timeout > 0`, tests that time out are **auto-appended** to `<layer>/luareg/ignore_lua_tests.lua` / `<layer>/creg/ignore_c_tests.lua` (lines 1531–1622) — i.e. it can mutate source-tree ignore-list files as a side effect of a timed run. This is worth flagging for CI: a CI run with `--timeout` could silently rewrite repo files (though only inside a fresh clone's workspace, not pushed anywhere, unless someone commits them back).

Not relevant if Jenkins nodes are CPU-only.

**Exit code behavior**: `run_action` itself doesn't call `os.exit()` on test failures — it just logs and updates counters/DB; the process exits 0 even if regression tests failed. (Non-zero `os.exit(1)` calls only occur for configuration errors: missing config at `loadConfigure`, line 543; unknown `--run-only` names, line 858; missing `--source-dir`, line 1657.) **This means a naive Jenkins `sh 'gkeyll runregression run check'` step will NOT fail the build on test failures** — the plan needs to add a step that queries the SQLite DB (or parses log output) for `nfail > 0` and exits non-zero explicitly.

## 2. Existing CI/docs references to regression tests

- **`ci/jenkins/README.md:270-273`** (the Jenkins-CI doc itself) already states the exact gap this task addresses: *"`make -j3 regression` — builds (does not execute) all regression tests, matching today's `.github/workflows/mac_build.yml` scope. **There is no automated regression-test runner yet; running a curated subset of regression tests is a follow-up.**"* This is essentially a TODO note left by whoever wrote the Jenkins setup.
- **`.github/workflows/mac_build.yml`** (GitHub Actions "Mac Build") only builds unit tests and regression *executables*, never runs them: `make -j 3 core-unit`, `core-regression`, `moments-unit`, `moments-regression`, `vlasov-unit`, `vlasov-regression`, `gyrokinetic-unit`, `gyrokinetic-regression`, `pkpm-regression` (no `pkpm-unit` step even). No `runregression` invocation anywhere.
- **`ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`** `buildAndTest()` (lines 13–46) does: clean → `mkdeps` script → `configure` script → `make -j3 check` (unit tests, built AND run) → `make -j3 regression` (regression tests built, NOT run). No `make install`, no `runregression` call.
- **No mention of `runregression`** anywhere in `.md`/`.yml`/Jenkinsfile files repo-wide (grep across README.md, ci/jenkins/README.md, .agents/skills — only the skill doc and the tool's own header comment reference it via the Lua tests/instructions, not CI).
- **`README.md:180-344`** documents the manual developer workflow: build via `make everything -j#` / `make gkeyll -j#`, run Lua inputs via `gkylsoft/gkeyll/bin/gkeyll <file>.lua`, build individual C regression tests via `make build/<layer>/creg/rt_*`, or all of them via `make regression -j#` / `make <layer>-regression -j#`. It documents running the compiled C regression binaries directly (each has its own `-h`-documented CLI, e.g. `-M -c/-d/-e` for MPI parallelism — see `.agents/skills/gkeyll_guide` table) but does **not** mention `runregression.lua` at all — i.e. the top-level README is currently silent on the Lua-orchestrated regression system.
- **Curated/short list of tests**: Yes — a **MOAT ("Mother Of All Tests")** list already exists and is exactly the kind of curated subset alluded to in the Jenkins README follow-up note. Files:
  - `<layer>/luareg/moat_lua.lua` and `<layer>/creg/moat_c.lua` for `moments`, `vlasov`, `gyrokinetic`, `pkpm` (8 files total; `core` has neither).
  - Selected via `runregression run --moat` / `runregression list --moat` (lines 706–711, 775–780, 2209–2210, 2232–2233).
  - Counts: moments 6 lua + 6 c, vlasov 4 + 4, gyrokinetic 3 + 3, pkpm 4 + 4 → **17 Lua + 17 C = 34 MOAT tests total**, e.g. `gyrokinetic/luareg/moat_lua.lua` lists `rt_gk_ion_sound_1x2v_p1`, `rt_gk_lbo_relax_1x2v_p1`, `rt_gk_sheath_bgk_1x2v_p1`.

## 3. How `gkylsoft/gkeyll/bin/gkeyll` gets built/installed

- **No plain `make install` target exists at the top level.** Top-level `Makefile` has only per-layer `*-install` targets, chained by dependency: `core-install` (line 277) ← `moments-install` (307, depends on `core-install`) ← `vlasov-install` (333) ← `gyrokinetic-install` (359) ← `pkpm-install` (385) ← **`gkeyll-install`** (line 405: `gkeyll-install: ${BUILD_APP}-install gkeyll`). `BUILD_APP` defaults to `pkpm` (`config.mak:12`, set by `configure` from `--app`, `configure:353`), so **`make gkeyll-install`** is the actual "build everything and install" command a developer/CI would run (the gkeyll_guide skill's "`make -j3 install`" phrasing is a slight simplification/possibly stale — the real target name is `gkeyll-install`).
  - Chain triggers: `core-install` also copies `config.mak` → `<prefix>/gkeyll/share/config.mak` and generates `<prefix>/gkeyll/share/Makefile` from `Makefile_for_ext_C_input` (Makefile lines 279–280) — **this is exactly the file `runregression.lua`'s `compileCTest` needs** to compile C regression tests on the fly, and the file `detectGpuBuild` reads for GPU detection.
  - `gkeyll-install` → `cd gkeyll && make -f Makefile-gkeyll install`, whose `install:` target (`gkeyll/Makefile-gkeyll:72`, deps `gkeyll-install cgkeyll-install gkeyll-header`) actually copies the compiled `gkeyll` executable and Lua stdlib into `${INSTALL_PREFIX}/gkeyll/bin/gkeyll` (see lines 71–90+ of that file) — this is literally what produces `gkylsoft/gkeyll/bin/gkeyll`.
- **Confirmed gap**: grepping `machines/*.sh`, `ci/jenkins/*`, and `.github/workflows/*.yml` for `"make install"` or any `*-install` target returns **nothing**. Neither Jenkins nor GitHub Actions currently runs any install step — `Jenkinsfile`'s `buildAndTest()` only runs `make -j3 check` then `make -j3 regression`, confirming the user's premise exactly. So **before `runregression` (or even the `gkeyll` binary) can be used at all in Jenkins, a `make -j3 gkeyll-install` (or equivalent) step must be added** to produce the installed `bin/gkeyll`, `share/Makefile`, and `share/config.mak`.

## 4. `make regression`/`creg` — plain C build, unrelated to runregression.lua

- Top-level `Makefile:414`: `regression: pkpm-regression gyrokinetic-regression vlasov-regression moments-regression core-regression`, each in turn (e.g. `core-regression`, line 274) does `cd <layer> && $(MAKE) -f Makefile-<layer> regression`.
- Inside e.g. `core/Makefile-core`: `REGS := $(patsubst %.c,../${BUILD_DIR}/core/%,$(wildcard creg/rt_*.c))` (line 34) and `regression: ${LLIB} ${SLLIB} ${REGS}` (line 49). Same pattern in `moments/`, `vlasov/`, `gyrokinetic/`, `pkpm/` Makefiles (per the earlier build/creg pattern rules in the top-level Makefile, e.g. `${BUILD_DIR}/moments/creg/%: moments/creg/%.c ...`). So `make regression` compiles **every `rt_*.c` file under `<layer>/creg/` into a standalone executable** under `build/<layer>/creg/rt_*` — nothing more. It does not run them, does not know about Lua tests, and does not touch SQLite/accepted baselines.
- **Relationship to `runregression.lua`**: they are two independent systems that both build/run the *same underlying C sources* (`<layer>/creg/rt_*.c`) but via different mechanisms:
  - `make regression` compiles once into `build/<layer>/creg/`, using the in-repo `Makefile-<layer>` build system (with dev-tree include paths); these binaries are left in `build/` for a developer to run manually (each supports its own `-h`-documented flags, e.g. `-M -c/-d/-e` for MPI/parallel decomposition, `-g` for GPU — see `rt_arg_parse.h`, e.g. `moments/creg/rt_arg_parse.h:98-102`).
  - `runregression.lua run` compiles **the same source files independently**, per-test, on demand, into ephemeral scratch dirs using the **installed** `share/Makefile` (i.e. it never touches or reuses `build/<layer>/creg/`), then runs them and diffs `.gkyl` output against accepted baselines, storing results in SQLite. It is a "wholly separate Lua-orchestrated harness" layered on top of the same test sources, plus it also natively discovers and runs the Lua-based tests (`<layer>/luareg/rt_*.lua`), which `make regression` has no concept of at all.
  - Practical implication for CI: `make -j3 regression` (already run by Jenkins) is **not a prerequisite** for `runregression run` — it's redundant/unrelated work for that purpose (though still useful as a fast compile-only smoke check independent of `make install`). The important prerequisite for `runregression` is `make install` (producing `share/Makefile`, `share/config.mak`, `bin/gkeyll`), not `make regression`.

## 5. Scale / practicality signals

Regression source-file counts (`find <layer>/{luareg,creg} -maxdepth 1 -name "rt_*.{lua,c}"`):

| Layer | luareg (Lua) | creg (C) |
|---|---|---|
| moments | 140 | 161 |
| vlasov | 122 | 119 |
| gyrokinetic | 30 | 110 |
| pkpm | 27 | 30 |
| core | — (no luareg dir) | 9 |
| **Total** | **319** | **429** |

So a full, unfiltered `gkeyll runregression run check` (all layers, no `--moat`, ignore-lists still applied) would attempt on the order of **~748 individual test cases minus ignore-list entries** (ignore lists strip roughly 31+41+18+25+20+19+9+10 ≈ 173 entries across layers, so effectively perhaps ~575 tests actually run) — each C test additionally pays a per-test **compile** cost (`make <testname>` from scratch per scratch dir, no shared object cache) before execution. There is no built-in "quick"/"smoke" flag *per se*, but the **`--moat` flag is exactly that**: a curated, maintained subset of only **34 tests total** (17 Lua + 17 C) across the four layers (moments 12, vlasov 8, gyrokinetic 6, pkpm 8) — explicitly documented as "the core acceptance set" (comment in `gyrokinetic/luareg/moat_lua.lua`). This is almost certainly the right default set for a Jenkins PR-gating job, given the full-suite cost.

No explicit runtime/duration comments were found in `runregression.lua` itself (no "long-running" annotations), but:
- `--timeout SECS` exists specifically to bound/kill long tests and auto-quarantine repeat offenders into the ignore lists (lines 1687–1691, 2236–2238) — the documented example workflow uses `--timeout 120` for both `create` and `check` (line 2167–2168), implying ~2 minutes/test is treated as a reasonable per-test ceiling by the tool's authors.
- MPI-parallel Lua tests (`--! {numProc=...}` header) are **skipped entirely** by `runregression` (not yet implemented) — so wall-clock cost is bounded by serial (or `--jobs N`) single-process runs only; no need to provision MPI process counts for CI sizing.
- `--jobs 0` auto-detects physical CPU count for intra-batch concurrency (C compilation and GPU reruns always serial), so Jenkins nodes with more cores can parallelize the MOAT run further if desired.

### Summary of gaps to close for the Jenkins plan
1. Add a `make -j3 gkeyll-install` (or `pkpm-install`/whichever scope is desired) step before any regression run — currently absent from both `Jenkinsfile` and `mac_build.yml`.
2. Add `gkeyll runregression configure --source-dir $WORKSPACE [--prefix $WORKSPACE/gkylsoft]` once per build (workspace is wiped every run per `ci/jenkins/README.md`, so this must run every time, not just once).
3. Run `gkeyll runregression run --moat check --timeout <N> [-j <cores>]` (34-test curated subset) rather than the full ~575–748 test corpus, matching the "curated subset ... follow-up" note already in `ci/jenkins/README.md:270-273`.
4. Add an explicit post-step to fail the Jenkins stage on regression failures, since `runregression` itself always exits 0 — need to inspect the per-layer SQLite DBs (`<prefix>/gkeyll-results/<layer>/regressiondb`, `RegressionMeta.nfail`) or grep the tool's stdout/log for failures and `exit 1` accordingly.
5. Decide whether/how to persist "accepted" baselines across CI runs (workspace is fully wiped each build per `ci/jenkins/README.md:258-263`, meaning `create` baselines would need to be checked in or fetched from a stable location rather than relying on a previous run's `gkylsoft/gkeyll-results/*-accepted/` — currently nothing in the repo commits accepted `.gkyl` baselines to git, so this is an open design question for the plan, not something already solved by existing infrastructure).</result>

questions.question: runregression's `check` mode diffs test output against a saved "accepted" baseline (default tolerance 1e-12). But Jenkins wipes the whole workspace (including gkylsoft/) every build, so there's no baseline left over from a prior run, and none is committed to the repo. How should CI get a baseline to check against?

options.label: Persistent per-node baseline (Recommended)
options.description: Keep a baseline cache outside the wiped workspace (e.g. a fixed dir on each Jenkins node), created once via `runregression run --moat create` when the node is set up, and manually refreshed by an admin whenever an intentional physics/algorithm change legitimately changes expected output. CI just runs `check` against it every build. Cheapest per-build cost; requires a manual bootstrap + occasional manual refresh step, documented in the README.

options.label: Build main first, then diff PR against it
options.description: Every CI run builds `main` and runs `runregression run --moat create` to establish a fresh baseline, then builds the PR branch and runs `check` against that. Avoids any stale/cross-machine baseline entirely (both runs happen back-to-back on the same node/toolchain), but roughly doubles build+test time per PR.

options.label: Skip baseline diffing for now
options.description: Just run `gkeyll runregression run --moat` (no create/check) so the 34 MOAT tests actually execute in CI -- catching crashes, timeouts, and compile failures -- without solving numerical-output diffing yet. Matches the README's existing "curated subset is a follow-up" note as a minimal first increment; full accept/check baseline diffing would be a later follow-up.

content.text: What would you like to clarify about the baseline strategy question?

I'm interested in the second option, but if a PR causes acceptable changes (because the physics changed, let's say), how would we tell Jenkins that the new results of a particular test are to be accepted?

Good question — worth surfacing because it changes the design meaningfully. Under "build main, then diff PR against it," any *legitimate* physics change necessarily shows up as a diff (it's being compared against the pre-change baseline from `main`), so the automatic check can't tell "intended change" from "bug" — that judgment call has to happen somewhere.

There are two common ways to handle it:

questions.question: Since a legitimate physics-changing PR will always show a diff against main's baseline, how should Jenkins let a human say "this diff is expected, don't block on it"?

options.label: Non-blocking report (Recommended)
options.description: The regression stage never fails the build. It just runs check, archives a readable diff summary (which MOAT tests changed, by how much) as a build artifact, and a human (PR author/reviewer) eyeballs it before merging. Unit tests (make check) remain the only hard gate. Simple, no new process to maintain, matches common practice for numerical codes where results are expected to shift often.

options.label: Per-PR acknowledgment file
options.description: A small checked-in file (e.g. ci/jenkins/expected_regression_diffs.txt) that a PR author edits to list which specific MOAT test names are expected to change in this PR, plus why. Jenkins fails the build only for diffs NOT in that list; listed diffs are logged but don't fail it. Gives a hard, auditable gate for unexpected diffs, at the cost of an extra manual step (and file to keep in sync) whenever physics intentionally changes.

# Run curated regression tests (MOAT) in Jenkins CI, diffed against `main`

## Context

Jenkins currently only builds and runs unit tests (`make -j3 check`) and
compiles (but never executes) regression-test executables (`make -j3
regression`). Gkeyll has a separate, more capable regression harness — the
Lua tool `gkeyll runregression` (`gkeyll/lua/Tool/runregression.lua`) — which
actually runs regression cases (both Lua `rt_*.lua` and C `rt_*.c` tests
across the `moments`/`vlasov`/`gyrokinetic`/`pkpm` layers) and numerically
diffs their `.gkyl` output against saved "accepted" baselines (default
tolerance `1e-12`, via the `check` subcommand), or saves new baselines (via
`create`). `ci/jenkins/README.md` already has a standing TODO for this
("running a curated subset of regression tests is a follow-up").

Two things make wiring this into Jenkins non-trivial:

1. **It needs the installed `gkeyll` binary.** `runregression` runs *as* the
   `gkeyll` Lua interpreter, and its C-test path compiles each test on the
   fly using `<prefix>/gkeyll/share/Makefile` — a file only produced by
   `make gkeyll-install` (Makefile:405, chained through
   `core/moments/vlasov/gyrokinetic/pkpm-install`), which Jenkins currently
   never runs at all.
2. **There's no baseline to check against.** `check` diffs against files
   under `<prefix>/gkeyll-results/<layer>/{luareg,creg}-accepted/`, but
   Jenkins wipes the whole workspace (including `gkylsoft/`) at the start of
   every build, and no baseline is committed to the repo (nor should it be:
   the default tolerance is `1e-12`, tight enough that a baseline generated
   on one machine/toolchain could easily fail to reproduce bit-for-bit on
   another — an actively bad idea across a growing set of independent
   Jenkins controllers/nodes, per [[jenkins-multi-controller]] if that memory
   exists, or just architecturally, since different nodes may have different
   compilers/BLAS/CPUs).

We're resolving (2) by building `main` fresh in the same CI run and using
that as the baseline (rather than a stale/committed one), and handling the
inevitable "legitimate physics change" case via a small, explicit, per-PR
acknowledgment file rather than silently overriding or hand-waving away
regression failures.

To keep scope bounded, this only wires up the **MOAT ("Mother Of All
Tests")** curated subset — 34 tests total (17 Lua + 17 C, ~6-12 per layer;
`<layer>/luareg/moat_lua.lua`, `<layer>/creg/moat_c.lua`) — not the full
~575-test corpus, matching the exact scope the README's existing TODO
already calls for.

## Approach

Per PR build, per node, after the existing unit-test/regression-build
stages:

1. **Build a `main` baseline in a side workspace.** Check out `main` (really
   `env.CHANGE_TARGET`, which is `main` for normal PRs) into
   `$WORKSPACE/_main_baseline/`, build its dependencies and install it into
   its own prefix (`$WORKSPACE/_main_baseline/gkylsoft`), then run
   `gkeyll runregression configure` + `run --moat create` there. This
   produces `.../gkeyll-results/<layer>/{luareg,creg}-accepted/` baseline
   files generated on *this exact node, this exact build* — so no
   cross-machine reproducibility risk.
2. **Install the PR's own build** (`make -j3 gkeyll-install`, into the
   existing `$WORKSPACE/gkylsoft`) and run `gkeyll runregression configure`
   there too (creates the same directory skeleton, empty).
3. **Copy the baseline in**: `cp -a` each layer's `luareg-accepted`/
   `creg-accepted` from the `_main_baseline` prefix into the PR's own prefix.
   These are just directories of plain `.gkyl` files, not tied to a DB, so
   this is a safe, simple copy.
4. **Run the MOAT suite against that baseline**: `gkeyll runregression run
   --moat check --timeout 300 --jobs 0` using the PR's installed `gkeyll`.
   This actually executes the 34 tests and diffs against the just-built
   `main` baseline, recording pass/fail/timeout/compile_fail per test in
   `<prefix>/gkeyll-results/<layer>/regressiondb` (SQLite; schema at
   runregression.lua:221-249 — status `-4`=compile_fail, `-3`=timeout,
   `0`=fail, `1`=pass). `runregression` itself always exits 0 regardless of
   test outcomes, so Jenkins can't just check the shell exit code here.
5. **Evaluate results against the acknowledgment file.** A small checked-in
   Lua script queries each layer's `regressiondb` for non-passing statuses,
   cross-references them against `ci/jenkins/expected_regression_diffs.txt`
   (see below), and exits non-zero — failing the Jenkins stage — only if any
   *unacknowledged* failure remains. Acknowledged ones are logged, not
   failed.

For a plain `main`-branch build (not a PR — no `CHANGE_TARGET` to diff
against), skip this whole apparatus; the existing unit-test/regression-build
stages are unaffected and remain main's coverage.

### The acknowledgment file: `ci/jenkins/expected_regression_diffs.txt`

A plain-text file, one `<layer>/<test-name>` per line (`#` comments allowed,
blank lines ignored), e.g.:

```
# Tests whose output is expected to change in this PR, and why.
# Clear this file back out once merged -- see ci/jenkins/README.md.
gyrokinetic/rt_gk_ion_sound_1x2v_p1   # updated collision-operator normalization
```

When a PR intentionally changes physics/algorithms such that a MOAT test's
output legitimately changes, the PR author adds a line here (the checker
script's own failure report will print the exact `<layer>/<test-name>` string
to copy in). This makes the CI gate meaningful for *unexpected* diffs while
letting intentional ones through without a human needing to click an
override in the Jenkins UI. Since the next PR's baseline is rebuilt from
`main` fresh every time, a merged intentional change simply stops showing up
as a diff for future PRs automatically — but a stale, un-cleared entry could
mask a *real* future regression on that same test name, so the file should
be emptied back out as part of (or right after) merging. This isn't enforced
by Jenkins as a hard gate (would make `main` builds flaky over a purely
process-hygiene issue); instead, add a small non-blocking check: on `main`
branch builds only (`!env.CHANGE_ID`), if this file has any non-comment
lines, `echo` a warning in the console reminding whoever's watching to clear
it.

## Changes

**`ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`**
- New function `buildRegressionBaseline(String mkdepsScript, String
  configureScript, String baseBranch)`, run inside `dir('_main_baseline')`:
  checks out `baseBranch` via an explicit `checkout([$class: 'GitSCM', ...])`
  against `https://github.com/gkeyllorg/gkeyll` (public repo, no credential
  needed for a read-only clone), then `mkdeps`/`configure` scripts with
  `PREFIX=$WORKSPACE/_main_baseline/gkylsoft`, `make -j3 gkeyll-install`,
  `gkeyll runregression configure --source-dir $WORKSPACE/_main_baseline
  --prefix $WORKSPACE/_main_baseline/gkylsoft`, `gkeyll runregression run
  --moat create --timeout 300`.
- In `buildAndTest`, after the existing `Regression build` stage, add:
  - `Install` stage: `make -j3 gkeyll-install`.
  - `Regression baseline (main)` stage: only `if (env.CHANGE_ID)`, calls
    `buildRegressionBaseline(mkdepsScript, configureScript,
    env.CHANGE_TARGET ?: 'main')`.
  - `Regression tests (MOAT)` stage: only `if (env.CHANGE_ID)` —
    `gkeyll runregression configure --source-dir $WORKSPACE --prefix
    $WORKSPACE/gkylsoft`, copy each layer's `*-accepted` dirs in from
    `_main_baseline`'s prefix, `gkeyll runregression run --moat check
    --timeout 300 --jobs 0`, then invoke the new checker script (below) and
    let its exit code fail the stage.
  - Update `Clean` to also `rm -rf "$WORKSPACE/_main_baseline"` so the
    side-workspace doesn't persist stale state across builds, matching the
    existing `gkylsoft`/`build` wipe.
  - Extend the final `archiveArtifacts` glob to also pick up
    `gkylsoft/gkeyll-results/**/*.txt` (failure reports) and
    `gkylsoft/gkeyll-results/**/regressiondb` for post-hoc debugging.
- Add the non-blocking "stale acknowledgment file" warning as a cheap step
  in `main`-branch builds (`!env.CHANGE_ID`).

**`ci/jenkins/check_regression_results.lua`** (new) — run via `gkeyll
ci/jenkins/check_regression_results.lua <resultsDir> [ackFile]`. For each of
the 4 layers, opens `<resultsDir>/<layer>/regressiondb` the same way
`runregression.lua` does (`require "sqlite3"`, `sql.open`), selects rows from
`RegressionData` with `status in (0, -3, -4)`, filters out any
`<layer>/<name>` present in the acknowledgment file, prints a clear
pass/ack/fail summary, and `os.exit(1)` if anything unacknowledged remains
(else `os.exit(0)`).

**`ci/jenkins/expected_regression_diffs.txt`** (new) — starts out with just
the header/instructions comment shown above, no active entries.

**`ci/jenkins/README.md`**
- Replace the existing "There is no automated regression-test runner yet;
  running a curated subset of regression tests is a follow-up" note (in
  "What the pipeline does") with a description of the new stages 8-9 (MOAT
  baseline build + check) and a short explanation of
  `expected_regression_diffs.txt` and when/how to use it (including the
  "clear it after merge" convention).
- Add a one-line cost note: PR builds now do two full dependency+source
  builds (PR + a fresh `main`), roughly doubling build time, in exchange for
  a same-machine baseline instead of a committed/stale one.

## Verification

- Inspect the Jenkinsfile diff by eye (same constraint as before — no local
  Groovy linter available).
- Manually run the new `gkeyll runregression configure/create/check`
  sequence locally once (outside Jenkins) against two local checkouts (a
  `main` clone and a scratch branch with a deliberately tweaked constant in
  one MOAT test) to confirm: (a) the baseline-copy step's directory layout
  assumption is correct, (b) the deliberately-changed test shows up as
  `status=0` (fail) in `regressiondb`, (c) adding its `<layer>/<name>` to
  `expected_regression_diffs.txt` makes `check_regression_results.lua` exit
  0, and removing it makes it exit 1.
- Push to a real PR against `main` and confirm: the new stages run, archive
  a `regressiondb`/failure report, and the build fails/passes as expected
  given the current (should be clean) MOAT baseline vs. PR state.
- Confirm the `main`-branch build path is unaffected (no new stages run,
  `env.CHANGE_ID` is unset there) and the stale-acknowledgment-file warning
  fires only when expected.

`<layer>/luareg/moat_lua.lua`, `<layer>/creg/moat_c.lua`) — not the full
~575-test corpus, matching the exact scope the README's existing TODO
already calls for.

## Approach

Per PR build, per node, after the existing unit-test/regression-build
stages:

1. **Build a `main` baseline in a side workspace.** Check out `main` (really
   `env.CHANGE_TARGET`, which is `main` for normal PRs) into
   `$WORKSPACE/_main_baseline/`, build its dependencies and install it into
   its own prefix (`$WORKSPACE/_main_baseline/gkylsoft`), then run
   `gkeyll runregression configure` + `run --moat create` there. This
   produces `.../gkeyll-results/<layer>/{luareg,creg}-accepted/` baseline
   files generated on *this exact node, this exact build* — so no
   cross-machine reproducibility risk.
2. **Install the PR's own build** (`make -j3 gkeyll-install`, into the
   existing `$WORKSPACE/gkylsoft`) and run `gkeyll runregression configure`
   there too (creates the same directory skeleton, empty).
3. **Move the baseline in**: `mv` each layer's `luareg-accepted`/
   `creg-accepted` from the `_main_baseline` prefix into the PR's own prefix
   (overwriting the empty dirs `configure` just created there). These are
   just directories of plain `.gkyl` files, not tied to a DB, and
   `_main_baseline` is scratch space nothing else reads afterward and that
   gets wiped at the start of the next build's `Clean` stage anyway — so
   moving instead of copying avoids briefly doubling disk usage on
   potentially large/numerous regression-output files, with no downside.
4. **Run the MOAT suite against that baseline**: `gkeyll runregression run
   --moat check --timeout 300 --jobs 0` using the PR's installed `gkeyll`.
   This actually executes the 34 tests and diffs against the just-built
   `main` baseline, recording pass/fail/timeout/compile_fail per test in
   `<prefix>/gkeyll-results/<layer>/regressiondb` (SQLite; schema at
   runregression.lua:221-249 — status `-4`=compile_fail, `-3`=timeout,
   `0`=fail, `1`=pass). `runregression` itself always exits 0 regardless of
   test outcomes, so Jenkins can't just check the shell exit code here.
5. **Evaluate results against the acknowledgment file.** A small checked-in
   Lua script queries each layer's `regressiondb` for non-passing statuses,
   cross-references them against `ci/jenkins/expected_regression_diffs.txt`
   (see below), and exits non-zero — failing the Jenkins stage — only if any
   *unacknowledged* failure remains. Acknowledged ones are logged, not
   failed.

For a plain `main`-branch build (not a PR — no `CHANGE_TARGET` to diff
against), skip this whole apparatus; the existing unit-test/regression-build
stages are unaffected and remain main's coverage.

### The acknowledgment file: `ci/jenkins/expected_regression_diffs.txt`

A plain-text file, one `<layer>/<test-name>` per line (`#` comments allowed,
blank lines ignored), e.g.:

```
# Tests whose output is expected to change in this PR, and why.
# Clear this file back out once merged -- see ci/jenkins/README.md.
gyrokinetic/rt_gk_ion_sound_1x2v_p1   # updated collision-operator normalization
```

When a PR intentionally changes physics/algorithms such that a MOAT test's
output legitimately changes, the PR author adds a line here (the checker
script's own failure report will print the exact `<layer>/<test-name>` string
to copy in). This makes the CI gate meaningful for *unexpected* diffs while
letting intentional ones through without a human needing to click an
override in the Jenkins UI. Since the next PR's baseline is rebuilt from
`main` fresh every time, a merged intentional change simply stops showing up
as a diff for future PRs automatically — but a stale, un-cleared entry could
mask a *real* future regression on that same test name, so the file should
be emptied back out as part of (or right after) merging. This isn't enforced
by Jenkins as a hard gate (would make `main` builds flaky over a purely
process-hygiene issue); instead, add a small non-blocking check: on `main`
branch builds only (`!env.CHANGE_ID`), if this file has any non-comment
lines, `echo` a warning in the console reminding whoever's watching to clear
it.

## Changes

**`ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`**
- New function `buildRegressionBaseline(String mkdepsScript, String
  configureScript, String baseBranch)`, run inside `dir('_main_baseline')`:
  checks out `baseBranch` via an explicit `checkout([$class: 'GitSCM', ...])`
  against `https://github.com/gkeyllorg/gkeyll` (public repo, no credential
  needed for a read-only clone), then `mkdeps`/`configure` scripts with
  `PREFIX=$WORKSPACE/_main_baseline/gkylsoft`, `make -j3 gkeyll-install`,
  `gkeyll runregression configure --source-dir $WORKSPACE/_main_baseline
  --prefix $WORKSPACE/_main_baseline/gkylsoft`, `gkeyll runregression run
  --moat create --timeout 300`.
- In `buildAndTest`, after the existing `Regression build` stage, add:
  - `Install` stage: `make -j3 gkeyll-install`.
  - `Regression baseline (main)` stage: only `if (env.CHANGE_ID)`, calls

  - `Regression tests (MOAT)` stage: only `if (env.CHANGE_ID)` —

1	# Jenkins CI for Gkeyll
2	
3	This sets up Jenkins (following the pattern used by
4	[SUNDIALS](https://github.com/llnl/sundials/tree/main/test/jenkins), adapted
5	for GitHub instead of Bitbucket) to build Gkeyll and run its unit tests on our
6	own persistent machines any time a pull request into `main` is opened or
7	updated.
8	
9	Like `.github/workflows/mac_build.yml`, every build starts from a clean git
10	checkout and builds its dependencies (`gkylsoft/`) from scratch into its own
11	Jenkins workspace via `machines/mkdeps.macos.sh` — but on our own persistent
12	hardware instead of an ephemeral GitHub-hosted runner, and it actually
13	executes the unit tests rather than just building them.
14	
15	Each Jenkins controller runs on whichever machine you install it on —
16	laptop, desktop, or workstation. `manauref_lt1` (manauref's laptop) was the
17	first one set up this way. Build nodes — a controller's own machine, plus any
18	others registered later, personal or shared — are added and configured the
19	same way (see step 4).
20	
21	This doc covers both adding a node under an *existing* controller (e.g.
22	`manauref_lt1`'s), and setting up your *own*, fully independent controller on
23	your own machine (step 3a) if you'd rather not grant that existing
24	controller's admin SSH access to your machine.
25	
26	## 1. Install Jenkins
27	
28	**macOS:**
29	
30	```
31	brew install jenkins-lts
32	brew services start jenkins-lts
33	```
34	
35	This pulls in `openjdk@21` as a dependency. `JENKINS_HOME` is
36	`~/.jenkins` (Homebrew's default on macOS — not
37	`/opt/homebrew/var/lib/jenkins`, despite what some older docs say). Get the
38	initial admin password with:
39	
40	```
41	cat ~/.jenkins/secrets/initialAdminPassword
42	```
43	
44	**Linux:** follow the [official Jenkins Linux install
45	instructions](https://www.jenkins.io/doc/book/installing/linux/) for your
46	distro (e.g. the `apt`/`yum` package repo), then start it via `systemctl
47	start jenkins` (most distros enable/start it automatically on install).
48	`JENKINS_HOME` is `/var/lib/jenkins` by default. Get the initial admin
49	password with:
50	
51	```
52	sudo cat /var/lib/jenkins/secrets/initialAdminPassword
53	```
54	
55	**Both:** Jenkins listens on `http://localhost:8080`. Open it, paste the
56	password, and install the "suggested plugins" set when prompted.
57	
58	## 2. Install additional plugins
59	
60	Manage Jenkins → Plugins → Available plugins, install:
61	
62	- **GitHub Branch Source** — lets Jenkins discover branches/PRs on a GitHub
63	  repo and is the GitHub equivalent of the Bitbucket Branch Source plugin
64	  SUNDIALS uses.
65	- **Collapsing Console Sections** (optional) — collapses long build log
66	  sections for readability, same as SUNDIALS' setup.
67	
68	## 3. Add a GitHub credential
69	
70	Jenkins needs read access to `gkeyllorg/gkeyll` to poll for branches and PRs:
71	
72	1. Create a GitHub Personal Access Token with `repo` scope (Settings →
73	   Developer settings → Personal access tokens on GitHub).
74	2. In Jenkins: Manage Jenkins → Credentials → System → Global credentials →
75	   Add Credentials → kind "GitHub personal access token" (or "Username with
76	   password", username = your GitHub username, password = the token).
77	
78	## 3a. Scope your controller to its own nodes
79	
80	`ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile` has a single `nodes` map listing every known build
81	node across every independent controller that builds this repo (yours and
82	anyone else's). This keeps that map a shared, PR-reviewable source of truth
83	— but it also means your controller must be told which of those labels it
84	actually owns agents for, or it will try to start a `node(label)` block for
85	someone else's node and hang forever waiting for an executor that will never
86	exist under your controller.
87	
88	Manage Jenkins → System → Global properties → check "Environment variables"
89	→ Add:
90	
91	- Name: `CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS`
92	- Value: a comma-separated list of the node label(s) *this controller* owns,
93	  e.g. `manauref_lt1`, or `alice_laptop,alice_workstation` if you register
94	  more than one node under your own controller.
95	
96	This is a controller-wide setting — set it once, regardless of how many
97	nodes your controller owns. If it's unset (or blank), the pipeline fails
98	fast with an error telling you to set it, rather than hanging; that's
99	expected the first time you set up a new controller.
100	
101	## 4. Add a build node
102	
103	Every machine that runs builds — including the controller's own machine — is
104	a Jenkins "node" with a label matching one used in `ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`'s
105	`nodes` map. This procedure is the same whether you're setting up
106	`manauref_lt1` (the first node) or adding another machine later.
107	
108	### 4.1. Register the node and label it
109	
110	- **This machine** (the controller itself, e.g. `manauref_lt1`): Manage
111	  Jenkins → Nodes → "Built-In Node" → Configure → Labels: add the label.
112	- **A separate machine** (e.g. a workstation): Manage Jenkins → Nodes → New
113	  Node → "Permanent Agent" → Launch method "Launch agents via SSH",
114	  host/credentials for that machine, and give it a label. Nothing to install
115	  there yourself — Jenkins pushes its agent jar over SSH. Make sure Java, a
116	  C/C++/Fortran toolchain, and `cmake` are present; `mkdeps` builds everything
117	  else from scratch per build.
118	
119	This label is what the Jenkinsfile's `node('<label>')` matches.
120	
121	### 4.2. Fix the node's `PATH`
122	
123	On **macOS**, Jenkins runs as a `launchd` service (via `brew services`),
124	which does **not** source your shell profile (`~/.zshrc`, `~/.zprofile`) —
125	so it starts with launchd's bare-bones default `PATH`
126	(`/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`) and can't find Homebrew tools like `cmake`,
127	even though `which cmake` works fine in your terminal.
128	
129	On **Linux**, the built-in node's agent process is started by `systemd`
130	(via the `jenkins` service), which likewise does not source your shell
131	profile — it uses whatever minimal `PATH` is baked into the unit's
132	environment, which typically misses anything installed under `/opt`, a
133	package manager outside the base distro repos, or `$HOME`. An SSH-launched
134	agent on another machine (either OS) has its own, similar set of environment
135	quirks to sort out, since `sshd` non-interactive sessions don't source
136	`~/.bashrc`/`~/.zshrc` either.
137	
138	Fix this per-node in Jenkins itself (not by editing the launchd plist,
139	systemd unit, or a shell profile) so it works the same way regardless of how
140	each node's agent process is started, and each node keeps its own value —
141	this generalizes cleanly as you add more, across OSes.
142	
143	Manage Jenkins → Nodes → `<label>` → Configure → Node Properties → check
144	"Environment variables" → Add:
145	
146	- Name: `PATH`
147	- Value: wherever this node's build tools (`cmake`, compilers, MPI, a
148	  `python` with `numpy`, etc.) actually live, e.g.:
149	  - macOS (`manauref_lt1`):
150	    `/opt/homebrew/bin:/opt/homebrew/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`
151	  - Linux: typically
152	    `/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`, plus anywhere your
153	    toolchain/MPI/Python were installed outside the base distro repos (e.g.
154	    `/opt/<something>/bin`, a Conda/venv `bin`, or `/usr/local/cuda/bin`).
155	
156	Don't assume this matches another node's value — especially across OSes.
157	
158	### 4.3. Personal machine or team machine?
159	
160	- **Personal computer** (like `manauref_lt1`): the multibranch job builds —
161	  i.e. executes — the code of any PR opened against the repo, on whichever
162	  node picks it up. On a personal machine you probably don't want to run
163	  other contributors' PR code, so restrict this node to PRs you authored: in
164	  `ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`, add `allowedPrAuthors: ['<your-github-username>']`
165	  to this node's entry in the `nodes` map. PR builds from any other author
166	  are skipped on this node (logged in the console, not failed); builds of
167	  `main` itself are unaffected, since there's no PR author to check there.
168	  Note this is a Jenkinsfile-level control, not a GitHub-side protection — it
169	  only takes effect once Jenkins has already scanned and started that node's
170	  branch of the pipeline.
171	- **Shared/team machine**: omit `allowedPrAuthors` from its entry — it will
172	  build PRs from anyone.
173	
174	### 4.4. Register the node in the Jenkinsfile
175	
176	Add (or confirm) an entry in the `nodes` map in `ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`,
177	using whichever `mkdeps`/`configure` scripts under `machines/` match that
178	node's OS:
179	
180	```groovy
181	def nodes = [
182	    'manauref_lt1': [mkdeps: 'mkdeps.macos.sh', configure: 'configure.macos.sh', allowedPrAuthors: ['manauref']],
183	    'workstation-node': [mkdeps: 'mkdeps.linux.sh', configure: 'configure.linux.cpu.sh'],
184	]
185	```
186	
187	Commit and push (a normal PR against `main`, same as any other change).
188	Adding a node's entry to this shared map doesn't by itself make any
189	controller build on it — only a controller whose `CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS`
190	(step 3a) includes this label will. The next PR build will then run on every
191	node your controller owns, in parallel (subject to each node's
192	`allowedPrAuthors`, if set).
193	
194	## 5. Nothing to pre-build
195	
196	Unlike an earlier version of this setup, the pipeline does **not** assume a
197	pre-built `gkylsoft/` on any node. Each build passes
198	`PREFIX=$WORKSPACE/gkylsoft` to that node's `mkdeps`/`configure` scripts, so
199	dependencies are built from scratch inside that build's own Jenkins
200	workspace — isolated from any manual checkout you have elsewhere, and safe
201	for concurrent builds of different branches/PRs on the same node (each gets
202	its own workspace, so its own `gkylsoft/`).
203	
204	The tradeoff is build time: expect each build to spend several extra minutes
205	building SuperLU/LuaJIT from source before it even gets to compiling Gkeyll,
206	same as `.github/workflows/mac_build.yml` does on GitHub's runners.
207	
208	You still need a working toolchain, `cmake`, and a `python` on `PATH` with
209	`numpy` installed (used to process the ADAS atomic data some gyrokinetic
210	unit tests, e.g. `ctest_dg_iz`/`ctest_dg_recomb`, need at runtime) on each
211	node for its `mkdeps` script to succeed — if you've built Gkeyll manually on
212	that machine before, you already have most of these:
213	
214	- **macOS**: Xcode command line tools (`xcode-select --install`) for the
215	  C/C++/Fortran toolchain, plus `cmake`/`python` (e.g. via Homebrew).
216	- **Linux**: a C/C++/Fortran toolchain (e.g. `build-essential` + `gfortran`
217	  on Debian/Ubuntu, or the equivalent group on your distro), plus `cmake` and
218	  a `python` with `numpy` from your package manager (or a Conda/venv install,
219	  as long as it's on the `PATH` set in step 4.2).
220	
221	## 6. Create the multibranch pipeline job
222	
223	New Item → name it (e.g. `gkeyll`) → **Multibranch Pipeline**.
224	
225	- **Branch Sources** → Add source → GitHub:
226	  - Credentials: the one added in step 3.
227	  - Repository HTTPS URL: `https://github.com/gkeyllorg/gkeyll`
228	  - Behaviors: "Discover branches" (at least `main`) and "Discover pull
229	    requests from origin". Add "Discover pull requests from forks" only if
230	    external contributors submit PRs from forks.
231	- **Build Configuration** → Mode: "by Jenkinsfile", Script Path:
232	  `ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`.
233	- **Scan Multibranch Pipeline Triggers** → check "Periodically if not
234	  otherwise run" → interval **2 minutes**.
235	
236	If your controller is behind NAT (as `manauref_lt1`'s is), GitHub can't push
237	a webhook to it. The periodic scan above is how Jenkins learns about
238	new/updated PRs instead — every 2 minutes it asks GitHub for changes and
239	kicks off a build if there are any. This means there's up to a ~2 minute
240	delay before a build starts, which is an acceptable tradeoff for not having
241	to run a public tunnel (e.g. ngrok) just to receive webhooks. If your
242	controller has a reachable public address, you can set up a GitHub webhook
243	instead for near-instant triggering — not covered here since none of our
244	controllers currently need it.
245	
246	Save. Jenkins will scan the repo, find `main` and any open PRs with a
247	Jenkinsfile, and start building them.
248	
249	## What the pipeline does
250	
251	First, the pipeline filters the shared `nodes` map down to just the label(s)
252	in this controller's own `CI_OWNED_NODE_LABELS` (step 3a) — failing fast if
253	that's not set. Then, per node this controller owns, in parallel (skipping a
254	node entirely if the PR's author isn't in that node's `allowedPrAuthors`,
255	when set):
256	
257	1. `printenv` — for debugging the build environment.
258	2. `make clean` and `rm -rf $WORKSPACE/gkylsoft` — the workspace persists
259	   across builds for a given branch/PR, so without this, a stale or (e.g.
260	   from a prior interrupted or racing build) corrupted file can look
261	   up-to-date and never get rebuilt/reinstalled, silently breaking the link
262	   or mixing old and new dependency files. Wiping both every run makes each
263	   build genuinely from scratch.
264	3. That node's `mkdeps` script (e.g. `machines/mkdeps.macos.sh`) — builds
265	   `gkylsoft/` from scratch into `$WORKSPACE/gkylsoft`.
266	4. That node's `configure` script (e.g. `machines/configure.macos.sh`) —
267	   generates `config.mak` pointing at that freshly-built `gkylsoft/`.
268	5. `make -j3 check` — builds **and runs** all unit tests (`core`, `moments`,
269	   `vlasov`, `gyrokinetic`, `pkpm`); a failing unit test fails the build.
270	6. `make -j3 regression` — builds (does not execute) all regression tests,
271	   matching today's `.github/workflows/mac_build.yml` scope. There is no
272	   automated regression-test runner yet; running a curated subset of
273	   regression tests is a follow-up.
274	7. Archives `build/**/*.log` so logs are downloadable from the Jenkins build
275	   page even on failure.
276

local function rununit_action(args, name)
   loadConfigure(args)
   local lua, cxx = list_unit_tests(args)
   log("Running unit tests ...\n\n")
   local tmStart = Time.clock()
   lume.each(lua, runLuaUnitTest)
   lume.each(cxx, runCxxUnitTest)
   log(string.format("All unit tests completed in %g secs\n", Time.clock() - tmStart))
end

-- ---- CLI parser -------------------------------------------------------------

local parser = argparse()
   :name("runregression")
   :require_command(true)
   :help_description_margin(30)
   :help_vertical_space(1)
   :description [[
Run Gkeyll regression tests across the hierarchical layer architecture
(moments -> vlasov -> gyrokinetic -> pkpm).

Each layer has Lua regression tests (luareg/) and C regression tests (creg/).
Results are stored in per-layer SQLite databases under gkeyll-results/.

Typical workflow:
  1. Build and install: make install -j4
  2. Configure: gkeyll runregression configure --source-dir /absolute/path/to/gkeyll/
  3. Create baselines: gkeyll runregression run create --timeout 120
  4. Check results:    gkeyll runregression run check  --timeout 120
  5. Layer-specific:   gkeyll runregression run moments check

C regression tests are compiled on-the-fly using the installed
share/Makefile (PREFIX/gkeyll/share/Makefile). No separate 'make regression'
step is needed.
]]

parser:flag("-v --verbose", "Print verbose messages as tests are run")

-- 'configure' command ---------------------------------------------------------
-- Sets up directories, databases, and writes ~/runregression.config.lua.
local c_conf = parser:command("configure", "Configure regression tests")
   :action(config_action)

c_conf:option("-s --source-dir",
   "REQUIRED. Absolute path to gkeyll source root\n"
   .. "(parent of moments/, vlasov/, gyrokinetic/, pkpm/).\n"
   .. "Example: --source-dir /path/to/gkeyll")
   :target("config_source_dir")
c_conf:option("-p --prefix",
   "Where to write gkeyll-results/.\n"
   .. "Auto-detected from config.mak if omitted.")
   :target("config_prefix")
c_conf:option("-m --mpiexec",
   "Full path to MPI executable.\n"
   .. "(MPI parallelism not yet implemented).")
   :target("config_mpiexec")
c_conf:flag("--drop-tables",
   "Drop and re-create all SQL tables\n"
   .. "(erases existing regression data).", false)

-- 'list' command --------------------------------------------------------------
-- Lists all regression tests that would be run (useful for inspection).
local c_list = parser:command("list", "List all regression tests")
   :action(list_action)
c_list:option("-r --run-only",

66	  local pre = "static const int32_t SQLITE_"
67	  for i=0,26    do t[#t+1] = pre..codes[i].."="..i..";\n" end

216	local sql_get_code = [=[
217	return function(stmt_or_value <opt_i>)
218	  local t = sql.sqlite3_<variant>_type(stmt_or_value <opt_i>)
219	  if t == sql.SQLITE_INTEGER then
220	    return sql.sqlite3_<variant>_int64(stmt_or_value <opt_i>)
221	  elseif t == sql.SQLITE_FLOAT then
222	    return sql.sqlite3_<variant>_double(stmt_or_value <opt_i>)
223	  elseif t == sql.SQLITE_TEXT then
224	    local nb = sql.sqlite3_<variant>_bytes(stmt_or_value <opt_i>)
225	    return ffi.string(sql.sqlite3_<variant>_text(stmt_or_value <opt_i>), nb)
226	  elseif t == sql.SQLITE_BLOB then
227	    local nb = sql.sqlite3_<variant>_bytes(stmt_or_value <opt_i>)
228	    return ffi.string(sql.sqlite3_<variant>_blob(stmt_or_value <opt_i>), nb)
229	  elseif t == sql.SQLITE_NULL then
230	    return nil
231	  else
232	    err("constraint", "unexpected SQLite3 type")
233	  end
234	end
235	]=]

237	local sql_set_code = [=[
238	return function(stmt_or_value, v <opt_i>)
239	  local t = type(v)
240	  if ffi.istype(int64_ct, v) then
241	    return sql.sqlite3_<variant>_int64(stmt_or_value <opt_i>, v)
242	  elseif t == "number" then
243	    return sql.sqlite3_<variant>_double(stmt_or_value <opt_i>, v)
244	  elseif t == "string" then
245	    return sql.sqlite3_<variant>_text(stmt_or_value <opt_i>, v, #v,
246	      transient)
247	  elseif t == "table" and getmetatable(v) == blob_mt then
248	    v = v[1]
249	    return sql.sqlite3_<variant>_blob(stmt_or_value <opt_i>, v, #v,
250	      transient)
251	  elseif t == "nil" then
252	    return sql.sqlite3_<variant>_null(stmt_or_value <opt_i>)
253	  else
254	    err("constraint", "unexpected Lua type")
255	  end

288	local open_modes = {
289	  ro = sql.SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY,
290	  rw = sql.SQLITE_OPEN_READWRITE,
291	  rwc = bit.bor(sql.SQLITE_OPEN_READWRITE, sql.SQLITE_OPEN_CREATE)

294	local function open(str, mode)
295	  mode = mode or "rwc"
296	  mode = open_modes[mode]
297	  if not mode then
298	    err("constraint", "argument #2 to open must be ro, rw, or rwc")
299	  end
300	  local aptr = ffi.new("sqlite3*[1]")
301	  -- Usually aptr is set even if error code, so conn always needs to be closed.
302	  local code = sql.sqlite3_open_v2(str, aptr, mode, nil)
303	  local conn = conn_ct(aptr[0], false)
304	  -- Must create this anyway due to conn:close() function.
305	  connstmt[conn] = setmetatable({}, { __mode = "k" })
306	  conncb[conn] = { scalar = {}, step = {}, final = {} }
307	  if code ~= sql.SQLITE_OK then
308	    local code, msg = codemsg(conn._ptr, code) -- Before closing!
309	    conn:close() -- Free resources, should not fail here in this case!
310	    err(code, msg)
311	  end
312	  return conn
313	end

315	function conn_mt:close() T_open(self)
316	   -- Close all stmt linked to conn.
317	  for k,_ in pairs(connstmt[self]) do if not k._closed then k:close() end end
318	   -- Close all callbacks linked to conn.
319	  for _,v in pairs(conncb[self].scalar) do v:free() end
320	  for _,v in pairs(conncb[self].step)   do v:free() end
321	  for _,v in pairs(conncb[self].final)  do v:free() end
322	  local code = sql.sqlite3_close(self._ptr)
323	  T_okcode(self._ptr, code)
324	  connstmt[self] = nil -- Table connstmt is not weak, need to clear manually.
325	  conncb[self] = nil
326	  self._closed = true -- Set only if close succeded.
327	end

333	function conn_mt:prepare(stmtstr) T_open(self)
334	  local aptr = ffi.new("sqlite3_stmt*[1]")
335	  -- If error code aptr NULL, so no need to close anything.
336	  local code = sql.sqlite3_prepare_v2(self._ptr, stmtstr, #stmtstr, aptr, nil)
337	  T_okcode(self._ptr, code)
338	  local stmt = stmt_ct(aptr[0], false, self._ptr, code)
339	  connstmt[self][stmt] = true
340	  return stmt
341	end

343	-- Connection exec, __call, rowexec --------------------------------------------
344	function conn_mt:exec(commands, get) T_open(self)
345	  local cmd1 = split(commands, ";")
346	  local res, n
347	  for i=1,#cmd1 do
348	    local cmd = trim(cmd1[i])
349	    if #cmd > 0 then
350	      local stmt = self:prepare(cmd)
351	      res, n = stmt:resultset(get)
352	      stmt:close()
353	    end
354	  end
355	  return res, n -- Only last record is returned.
356	end

358	function conn_mt:rowexec(command) T_open(self)
359	  local stmt = self:prepare(command)
360	  local res = stmt:_step()
361	  if stmt:_step() then
362	    err("misuse", "multiple records returned, 1 expected")
363	  end
364	  stmt:close()
365	  if res then
366	    return unpack(res)
367	  else
368	    return nil
369	  end
370	end

372	function conn_mt:__call(commands, out) T_open(self)
373	  out = out or print
374	  local cmd1 = split(commands, ";")
375	  for c=1,#cmd1 do
376	    local cmd = trim(cmd1[c])
377	    if #cmd > 0 then
378	      local stmt = self:prepare(cmd)
379	      local ret, n = stmt:resultset()
380	      if ret then -- All the results get handled, not only last one.
381	        out(unpack(ret[0])) -- Headers are printed.
382	        for i=1,n do
383	          local o = {}
384	          for j=1,#ret[0] do
385	            local v = ret[j][i]
386	            if type(v) == "nil" then v = "" end -- Empty strings for NULLs.
387	            o[#o+1] = tostring(v)
388	          end
389	          out(unpack(o))
390	        end
391	      end
392	      stmt:close()
393	    end
394	  end
395	end
